claims.source: Quantification of relative mRNA expression by qRT-PCR revealed that Slc6a14 is expressed predominantly in the wild-type mouse colon (C57BL/6N Figure 1a).
claims.evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1a demonstrating highest expression in colon compared to other tissues.

claims.claim: SLC6A14 was localized at the apical pole on the apical surface in mouse colonic organoids.
claims.source: We found that SLC6A14 was localized at the apical pole on the apical surface, as expected (Figure 1b).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by confocal microscopy of colonic organoids transduced with SLC6A14-GFP showing apical localization.

claims.claim: The Slc6a14(-/y) mice exhibited ~ 75% reduction in apical arginine transport compared to wild-type mice.
claims.source: Interestingly, we found that the Slc6a14 (-/y) mice exhibited ~ 75% reduction in apical arginine transport (Figure 1e), suggesting that Slc6a14 constitutes a major apical arginine uptake pathway in the mouse colon.
claims.evidence: Measured using ex vivo closed loop assay with 3H-arginine uptake, shown in Figure 1e.

claims.claim: Slc6a14 constitutes a major apical arginine uptake pathway in the mouse colon.
claims.source: Interestingly, we found that the Slc6a14 (-/y) mice exhibited ~ 75% reduction in apical arginine transport (Figure 1e), suggesting that Slc6a14 constitutes a major apical arginine uptake pathway in the mouse colon.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the 75% reduction in arginine transport when Slc6a14 is knocked out.

claims.claim: The steady state levels of arginine were lower in the Slc6a14 knock-out colonic epithelium compared to wild-type epithelium.
claims.source: We performed mass spectrometry using freshly lysed tissue, and found that the steady state levels of arginine were indeed lower in the Slc6a14 knock-out colonic epithelium (steady state L-arginine = L-arginine/(L-citrulline + L-ornithine)), compared to wild-type epithelium (Figure 1f).
claims.evidence: Measured by mass spectrometry of freshly lysed tissue, shown in Figure 1f as arginine bioavailability.

claims.claim: Decrease in amino acid uptake across the colonic epithelium did not affect serum amino acid levels.
claims.source: Interestingly, decrease in amino acid uptake across the colonic epithelium did not affect serum amino acid levels (Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by serum amino acid analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The F508del mutation in mice results in an intestinal phenotype of varying severity, which is dependent on the genetic background of the mouse.
claims.source: It is known that the F508del mutation in mice results in an intestinal phenotype of varying severity, which is dependent on the genetic background of the mouse (Rozmahel et al., 1996).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Rozmahel et al., 1996.

claims.claim: Disruption of Slc6a14 in CF mice (Cftr(F508del/F508del) Slc6a14(-/y)) led to a further reduction in weight gain and BMI post weaning (day 34), relative to age matched controls.
claims.source: As shown in Figure 2, disruption of Slc6a14 in CF mice (Cftr(F508del/F508del) Slc6a14(-/y)) led to a further reduction in weight gain and BMI post weaning (day 34), relative to age matched controls, (Cftr(F508del/F508del) Slc6a14(+/y)) (Figure 2a,b,c, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by weight and BMI measurements shown in Figure 2a, b, c.

claims.claim: The defect in weight gain in double mutant mice was temporary in nature, with the double mutant mice recovering to the same weight as the F508del mice by 56 days in age.
claims.source: While this defect in weight gain was temporary in nature, with the double mutant mice recovering to the same weight as the F508del mice by 56 days in age, it was associated with increased mortality during this period (Figure 2d).
claims.evidence: Shown by weight tracking data and survival curves in Figure 2d.

claims.claim: The defect in weight gain in double mutant mice was associated with increased mortality during the post-weaning period.
claims.source: While this defect in weight gain was temporary in nature, with the double mutant mice recovering to the same weight as the F508del mice by 56 days in age, it was associated with increased mortality during this period (Figure 2d).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by Kaplan-Meier survival curves in Figure 2d showing significantly lower survival in double mutant mice.

claims.claim: CF mice exhibit reduced weights relative to their wild-type siblings early in life after weaning.
claims.source: It has been previously reported that CF mice exhibit reduced weights relative to their wild-type siblings early in life after weaning (van Doorninck et al., 1995), and we confirmed this defect in the current experiment at day 34 after birth, in the Cftr(F508del/F508del) mice (Figure 2).
claims.evidence: Confirmed by weight measurements at day 34 shown in Figure 2, and supported by citation to van Doorninck et al., 1995.

claims.claim: The CF-related smooth muscle thickening phenotype in the distal ileum and colon was worse when Slc6a14 was disrupted.
claims.source: Interestingly, we also found that the CF-related smooth muscle thickening phenotype in the distal ileum and colon was worse when Slc6a14 was disrupted (Figure 3a,b,c and d).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by histological analysis shown in Figure 3a-d showing increased smooth muscle area in double mutant mice.

claims.claim: cAMP induced CFTR-mediated fluid accumulation was decreased in intestinal segments derived from mice, homozygous for F508del-Cftr.
claims.source: As previously reported, cyclic AMP (cAMP) induced CFTR-mediated fluid accumulation was decreased in intestinal segments derived from mice, homozygous for F508del-Cftr (Figure 4a and b).
claims.evidence: Measured by in-situ closed loop assay shown in Figure 4a and b.

claims.claim: Disruption of Slc6a14 in the CF mice further worsened the secretory defect.
claims.source: Importantly, disruption of Slc6a14 in the CF mice, further worsened this secretory defect (Figure 4b).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by in-situ closed loop assay showing lower fluid secretion in double mutant mice compared to F508del mice, shown in Figure 4b.

claims.claim: Slc6a14 disruption alone impaired cAMP-induced secretion relative to that in wild-type (C57BL/6N background) siblings.
claims.source: Interestingly, Slc6a14 disruption alone impaired cAMP-induced secretion relative to that in wild-type (C57BL/6N background) siblings (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by closed loop assay in C57BL/6N background mice shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The decrease in fluid secretion in Slc6a14 knockout mice was not due to change in Cftr mRNA expression.
claims.source: This decrease in fluid secretion was not due to change in Cftr mRNA expression (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), and the basis for this change is investigated in subsequent studies.
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by qRT-PCR showing no significant difference in Cftr mRNA levels, shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The FIS response was significantly lower in the colonic organoids from double mutant mice (CftrF508del/F508del; Slc6a14(-/y)), compared to the F508del-CF mice.
claims.source: As expected from the above 'closed loop' studies, the FIS response was significantly lower in the colonic organoids from double mutant mice (CftrF508del/F508del; Slc6a14(-/y)), compared to the F508del-CF mice (Figure 4c and d).
claims.evidence: Measured by forskolin-induced swelling assay in colonic organoids, shown in Figure 4c and d.

claims.claim: SLC6A14 is a major apical arginine transporter in the colonic epithelium of wild-type and F508del mice, on the FVB background.
claims.source: We confirmed that SLC6A14 is a major apical arginine transporter in the colonic epithelium of wild-type and F508del mice, on the FVB background (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by ex vivo closed loop arginine uptake assay shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Acute pre-addition of L-arginine (1 mM) on the apical surface increased the residual, cAMP-activated function of F508del-CFTR in split-open organoids derived from F508del-mice at 27°C.
claims.source: Importantly, we found that acute pre-addition of L-arginine (1 mM) on the apical surface, increased the residual, cAMP-activated function of F508del-CFTR in split-open organoids derived from F508del-mice at 27°C (Figure 6a and b).
claims.evidence: Measured by ACC assay in split-open organoids at 27°C, shown in Figure 5c and d (note: text references Figure 6a and b but should be Figure 5c and d based on figure numbering).

claims.claim: The arginine-dependent enhancement effect on F508del-CFTR function was lacking in tissues obtained from the double mutant mice, lacking SLC6A14.
claims.source: This arginine-dependent enhancement effect was lacking in tissues obtained from the double mutant mice, lacking SLC6A14 (Figure 5a and b).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by ACC assay showing no enhancement with arginine in double mutant organoids, shown in Figure 5d.

claims.claim: F508del-CFTR channel function upon FSK stimulation was still detectable at 37°C, albeit reduced in comparison to measurements acquired at 27°C.
claims.source: F508del-CFTR channel function upon FSK stimulation was still detectable at this temperature, albeit reduced in comparison to measurements acquired at 27°C (Figure 5e,f), reflecting the sensitivity of the ACC assay.
claims.evidence: Measured by ACC assay at 37°C shown in Figure 5e and f.

claims.claim: Residual mutant F508del-CFTR function at 37°C was enhanced by pre-addition of L-arginine on the apical surface in the Cftr(F508del/F508del) murine organoids, but not from those derived from the tissue of double mutant (CftrF508del/F508del; Slc6a14(-/y)) mice.
claims.source: Further, as in the preceding experiments, this residual mutant CFTR function, was enhanced by pre-addition of L-arginine on the apical surface in the Cftr(F508del/F508del) murine organoids, but not from those derived from the tissue of double mutant (CftrF508del/F508del; Slc6a14(-/y)) mice (Figure 5e,f).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by ACC assay at 37°C shown in Figure 5e and f.

claims.claim: The cAMP-stimulated CFTR function was lower in the double mutant-derived organoids compared to F508del organoids.
claims.source: Also, the cAMP-stimulated CFTR function was lower in the double mutant-derived organoids.
claims.evidence: Inferred from ACC assay data comparing F508del and double mutant organoids.

claims.claim: Over-expression of SLC6A14 did not affect the processing of the temperature rescued F508del-CFTR protein.
claims.source: We found that over-expression of SLC6A14 did not affect the processing of the temperature rescued F508del-CFTR protein (Figure 5—figure supplement 3), nor did it alter the cell surface stability of the rescued protein.
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by western blot analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: Over-expression of SLC6A14 did not alter the cell surface stability of the temperature rescued F508del-CFTR protein.
claims.source: We found that over-expression of SLC6A14 did not affect the processing of the temperature rescued F508del-CFTR protein (Figure 5—figure supplement 3), nor did it alter the cell surface stability of the rescued protein.
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by cycloheximide chase assay shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: There was no significant effect of SLC6A14 expression on the processing or stability of human F508del-CFTR.
claims.source: Therefore, there was no significant effect of SLC6A14 expression on the processing or stability of human F508del-CFTR.
claims.evidence: Concluded from western blot and cycloheximide chase experiments in BHK cells.

claims.claim: Reciprocal co-immunoprecipitation of SLC6A14 and F508del-CFTR was not detected.
claims.source: As shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4, we did not detect reciprocal co-immunoprecipitation of the two membrane proteins.
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claims.claim: Induced NOS (iNOS) is expressed in mouse colonic tissue.
claims.source: As shown in Figure 6a, the SLC6A14 substrate, arginine, is converted to nitric oxide (NO) by nitric oxide synthase (NOS), and we found that induced NOS (iNOS) is expressed in mouse colonic tissue (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by PCR showing iNOS mRNA expression in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Nitric oxide activates F508del-CFTR channel function.
claims.source: In the current work, we showed nitric oxide (NO) also activates F508del-CFTR channel function.
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by experiments with NO donor GSNO enhancing forskolin response.

claims.claim: The forskolin response measured in split-open organoids from CftrF508del/F508del mice was enhanced by the NO donor GSNO.
claims.source: Specifically, the forskolin response measured in split-open organoids from CftrF508del/F508del mice was enhanced by the NO donor GSNO (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by ACC assay with GSNO treatment shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: The positive effect of arginine on forskolin activated F508del channel function was reduced by pretreatment with the iNOS inhibitor 1400W in organoids derived from CftrF508del/F508del mice.
claims.source: We found that the positive effect of arginine on forskolin activated F508del channel function was reduced by pretreatment with the iNOS inhibitor 1400W in organoids derived from CftrF508del/F508del mice.
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by ACC assay with 1400W pretreatment shown in Figure 6b and c.

claims.claim: The 1400W sensitive effect of arginine on F508del-CFTR was dependent on SLC6A14 expression.
claims.source: Further the 1400W sensitive effect of arginine was dependent on SLC6A14 expression (Figure 6b,c).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by comparing effects in F508del vs double mutant organoids in Figure 6b and c.

claims.claim: Colonic epithelial tissue derived from Slc6a14 knock-out mice exhibited lower constitutive NO levels.
claims.source: As shown in Figure 6d, colonic epithelial tissue derived from Slc6a14 knock-out mice exhibited lower constitutive NO levels.
claims.evidence: Measured by DAF-FM fluorescence assay shown in Figure 6d.

claims.claim: There was an increase in NO production evoked by acute addition of arginine (1 mM) to the apical surface of split-open colonic organoids obtained from wild-type mice, but this increase was abrogated in split-open organoids generated from Slc6a14(-/y) littermates.
claims.source: Interestingly, while there was an increase in NO production evoked by acute addition of arginine (1 mM) to the apical surface of split-open colonic organoids obtained from wild-type mice, this increase was abrogated in split-open organoids generated from Slc6a14(-/y) littermates (Figure 6e–f).
claims.evidence: Measured by DAF-FM fluorescence assay shown in Figure 6e and f.

claims.claim: Slc6a14-mediated arginine uptake is important for NO synthesis.
claims.source: Altogether, these data show that Slc6a14-mediated arginine uptake is important for NO synthesis, and hence NO mediated signaling to the CFTR channel.
claims.evidence: Concluded from experiments showing reduced NO levels and arginine-stimulated NO production in Slc6a14 knockout mice.

claims.claim: Over-expression of SLC6A14 via lentivirus transduction conferred increased constitutive levels of NO.
claims.source: Conversely, over-expression of SLC6A14 via lentivirus transduction conferred increased constitutive levels of NO and enhanced the increase in cytosolic NO after addition of arginine to the apical surface of split-open organoids (Figure 6g–i).
claims.evidence: Measured by DAF-FM fluorescence in SLC6A14-GFP transduced organoids shown in Figure 6g-i.

claims.claim: Over-expression of SLC6A14 enhanced the increase in cytosolic NO after addition of arginine to the apical surface of split-open organoids.
claims.source: Conversely, over-expression of SLC6A14 via lentivirus transduction conferred increased constitutive levels of NO and enhanced the increase in cytosolic NO after addition of arginine to the apical surface of split-open organoids (Figure 6g–i).
claims.evidence: Measured by DAF-FM fluorescence in SLC6A14-GFP transduced organoids shown in Figure 6g-i.

claims.claim: PKA-mediated activation of Wt-CFTR function can be enhanced by the NO donors GSNO and SNP, and by the downstream signaling molecule cGMP.
claims.source: Using the ACC assay (Ahmadi et al., 2017), to measure CFTR channel function, we found that PKA-mediated activation of Wt-CFTR function can be enhanced by the NO donors GSNO and SNP, and by the downstream signaling molecule cGMP.
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by ACC assay in Caco-2 cells shown in Figure 7b and c.

claims.claim: The effect of GSNO on PKA-activated CFTR channel function is abolished in presence of protein kinase G (PKG) inhibitors Rp-8-pCPT-cGMPS and KT5823.
claims.source: This effect of GSNO on PKA-activated CFTR channel function is abolished in presence of protein kinase G (PKG) inhibitors Rp-8-pCPT-cGMPS and KT5823 (Figure 7b,c,d).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by ACC assay in Caco-2 cells with PKG inhibitors shown in Figure 7b, c, and d.

claims.claim: PKA-dependent channel activity of CFTR is enhanced by NO-mediated activation of PKG in Caco-2 colonic epithelial cell line.
claims.source: Thus, we show that PKA-dependent channel activity of CFTR is enhanced by NO-mediated activation of PKG, in this colonic epithelial cell line, highlighting the importance of this signaling pathway for CFTR function in a model of human colon.
claims.evidence: Concluded from experiments with NO donors and PKG inhibitors in Caco-2 cells.

claims.claim: CFTR function was enhanced by pre-activation of SLC6A14 with arginine, only in the Caco-2 cell line over-expressing SLC6A14.
claims.source: Using the CFTR functional assay described above, we found that CFTR function (measured as CFTRinh-172 response) was enhanced by pre-activation of SLC6A14 with arginine, only in the Caco-2 cell line over-expressing SLC6A14.
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by FLIPR membrane potential assay in Caco-2 cells shown in Figure 7e and f.

claims.claim: Enhancement of CFTR function by SLC6A14-mediated arginine transport could be inhibited by PKG specific inhibitors Rp-8-pCPT-cGMPS and KT5823, as well as the iNOS inhibitor 1440W.
claims.source: This enhancement of CFTR function by SLC6A14-mediated arginine transport could be inhibited by PKG specific inhibitors Rp-8-pCPT-cGMPS and KT5823, as well as the iNOS inhibitor 1440W (Figure 7e,f).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by FLIPR membrane potential assay in Caco-2 cells with inhibitors shown in Figure 7e and f.

claims.claim: SLC6A14-mediated arginine transport can enhance CFTR function via the NO signaling pathway, in Caco-2 cells.
claims.source: Taken together, we show that SLC6A14-mediated arginine transport can enhance CFTR function via the NO signaling pathway, in Caco-2 cells.
claims.evidence: Concluded from experiments showing arginine enhancement of CFTR function that is blocked by iNOS and PKG inhibitors.

claims.claim: Pre-treatment of split-open organoids from double mutant mice with membrane permeable cGMP (8Br-cGMP) enhanced forskolin-activated F508del-CFTR channel activity partially towards that observed in tissues from F508del mice with native SLC6A14 expression at 27°C.
claims.source: Interestingly, we found that pre-treatment of split-open organoids from double mutant mice, with membrane permeable cGMP (8Br-cGMP), enhanced forskolin-activated F508del-CFTR channel activity partially towards that observed in tissues from F508del mice with native SLC6A14 expression (Figure 8a,b).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by ACC assay at 27°C shown in Figure 8a and b.

claims.claim: The partial rescue effect induced by 8Br-cGMP pre-treatment was recapitulated at physiological temperature (37°C) in the organoid swelling assay.
claims.source: Importantly, the partial rescue effect induced by 8Br-cGMP pre-treatment was recapitulated at physiological temperature in the organoid swelling assay (Figure 8c,d).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by forskolin-induced swelling assay at 37°C shown in Figure 8c and d.

claims.claim: Pre-treatment of organoids from double mutant mice with cGMP restored forskolin-induced swelling (FIS) to approximately 50% of the swelling measured in F508del-CFTR organoids, at 37°C.
claims.source: Specifically, pre-treatment of organoids from double mutant mice with cGMP restored forskolin-induced swelling (FIS) to approximately 50% of the swelling measured in F508del-CFTR organoids, at 37°C.
claims.evidence: Quantified from organoid swelling assay data shown in Figure 8d.

claims.claim: The arginine transport activity of SLC6A14 and the downstream signaling via NO regulated cGMP plays an important role in modifying F508del-CFTR channel function and F508del-CFTR-mediated secretion.
claims.source: Together, these findings support the hypothesis that the arginine transport activity of SLC6A14 and the downstream signaling via NO regulated cGMP plays an important role in modifying F508del-CFTR channel function and F508del-CFTR-mediated secretion.
claims.evidence: Concluded from experiments showing cGMP rescue of F508del-CFTR function in double mutant organoids.

claims.claim: SLC6A14 is a major arginine transporter on the apical surface of the colonic epithelium in mice modeling the major CF-causing mutation F508del.
claims.source: This work provides a mechanism whereby SLC6A14, previously identified as a genetic modifier of CF disease severity, can ameliorate the primary CF-causing defect. We found that SLC6A14 is a major arginine transporter on the apical surface of the colonic epithelium and in mice modeling the major CF-causing mutation F508del, and its arginine transport function can ameliorate the basic defect in fluid secretion.
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by arginine uptake assays and functional studies throughout the manuscript.

claims.claim: SLC6A14's arginine transport function can ameliorate the basic defect in fluid secretion in CF mice.
claims.source: This work provides a mechanism whereby SLC6A14, previously identified as a genetic modifier of CF disease severity, can ameliorate the primary CF-causing defect. We found that SLC6A14 is a major arginine transporter on the apical surface of the colonic epithelium and in mice modeling the major CF-causing mutation F508del, and its arginine transport function can ameliorate the basic defect in fluid secretion.
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by fluid secretion assays and organoid swelling studies showing worsened defects when SLC6A14 is absent.

claims.claim: SLC6A14 has been identified as a genetic modifier of multiple CF disease outcomes, including meconium ileus, lung disease, and the age of first infection by Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
claims.source: SLC6A14 has been identified as a genetic modifier of multiple CF disease outcomes, including meconium ileus (Sun et al., 2012), lung disease (Corvol et al., 2015) and the age of first infection by Pseudomonas aeruginosa (Li et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Sun et al., 2012; Corvol et al., 2015; and Li et al., 2014.

claims.claim: The pleiotropic effect of SLC6A14 supports the hypothesis that it modifies the basic defect responsible for disease in multiple organs, namely the defect in anion conduction.
claims.source: This pleiotropic effect supports the hypothesis that it modifies the basic defect responsible for disease in multiple organs, namely the defect in anion conduction.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation that SLC6A14 affects multiple CF disease outcomes.

claims.claim: The intestinal phenotypes associated with the primary CF defect in mice, namely defective secretory capacity with thickened smooth muscle, were worsened by disruption of Slc6a14 expression.
claims.source: In support of the above hypothesis, we found that the intestinal phenotypes associated with the primary CF defect in mice, namely defective secretory capacity with thickened smooth muscle, were worsened by disruption of Slc6a14 expression.
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by fluid secretion assays and histological analysis showing worsened phenotypes in double mutant mice.

claims.claim: Disruption of Slc6a14 expression in mice bearing Wt-CFTR did not cause profound changes in colonic morphology, function or mouse survival.
claims.source: Interestingly, disruption of Slc6a14 expression in mice bearing Wt-CFTR did not cause profound changes in colonic morphology (IMPC, 2018), function or mouse survival.
claims.evidence: Supported by reference to IMPC, 2018 and confirmed by the authors' observations.

claims.claim: Disruption of Slc6a14 did impair arginine uptake across the apical membrane of colonic epithelium in Wt-Cftr C57Bl/6 mice.
claims.source: However, disruption of Slc6a14 did impair arginine uptake across the apical membrane of colonic epithelium in Wt-Cftr C57Bl/6 mice (Figure 1e), and impaired cAMP-mediated fluid secretion (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by arginine uptake assay in Figure 1e and fluid secretion assay in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: This arginine transporter on the apical membrane of colonic epithelium has a dominant role in CFTR regulation rather than nutrient uptake.
claims.source: Together, these observations support the hypothesis that this arginine transporter on the apical membrane of colonic epithelium has a dominant role in CFTR regulation rather than nutrient uptake, as amino acid uptake normally occurs in the small intestine.
claims.evidence: Inferred from observations that Slc6a14 knockout affects CFTR function but not serum amino acid levels, and that amino acid uptake normally occurs in the small intestine.

claims.claim: The negative consequences of the F508del mutation on folding and assembly of the mouse CFTR protein are somewhat less severe than in human CFTR protein, hence there is residual epithelial expression and function being detected in this organism.
claims.source: In contrast to the consequences of the F508del mutation in the human CFTR protein, the negative consequences of this mutation in folding and assembly of the mouse CFTR protein are somewhat less severe, hence there is residual epithelial expression and function being detected in this organism (Scholte et al., 2004; van Doorninck et al., 1995; Wilke et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Scholte et al., 2004; van Doorninck et al., 1995; and Wilke et al., 2011.

claims.claim: A significant amount of the mutant mouse F508del-CFTR protein will reach the surface and function.
claims.source: As previously published, this reflects a less deleterious effect of the mutation on the folding, assembly and maturation, such that a significant amount of the mutant mouse protein (still less that wild-type) will reach the surface and function (French et al., 1996; Rozmahel et al., 1996; Scholte et al., 2004; van Doorninck et al., 1995).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to French et al., 1996; Rozmahel et al., 1996; Scholte et al., 2004; and van Doorninck et al., 1995.

claims.claim: The extent of modulation by SLC6A14 in the colonic epithelium of CF patients with the F508del mutation will depend on its residual expression levels at the apical membrane of this epithelium, or the abundance of this mutant at the cell surface after correction with Lumacaftor.
claims.source: We predict that the extent of modulation by SLC6A14 in the colonic epithelium of CF patients with the F508del mutation will depend on its residual expression levels at the apical membrane of this epithelium, or the abundance of this mutant at the cell surface after correction with Lumacaftor.
claims.evidence: This is a prediction based on the findings that SLC6A14 modulates F508del-CFTR function.

claims.claim: The modulation of F508del-CFTR by SLC6A14 is dependent, at least in part, on arginine-mediated NO production and PKG activation.
claims.source: Our findings suggest that the modulation of F508del-CFTR by SLC6A14 is dependent, at least in part, on arginine-mediated NO production and PKG activation.
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by experiments showing that iNOS and PKG inhibitors block the effect of arginine on F508del-CFTR function.

claims.claim: The role of the arginine-NO pathway has been well studied in models of CF.
claims.source: The role of the arginine-NO pathway has been well studied in models of CF (Grasemann et al., 2011; Grasemann et al., 1997; Grasemann and Ratjen, 2012; Grasemann et al., 2005; Oliynyk et al., 2013; Poschet et al., 2007; Scott et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: Supported by multiple citations to studies of the arginine-NO pathway in CF.

claims.claim: The downstream regulators of the arginine-NO pathway, cGMP and PKG, can enhance wild-type and mutant CFTR channel function and trafficking.
claims.source: At the molecular level, it is known that the downstream regulators of this pathway, cGMP and PKG, can enhance wild-type and mutant CFTR channel function and trafficking (Golin-Bisello et al., 2005; Leier et al., 2012; Poschet et al., 2007; Vaandrager et al., 1997).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Golin-Bisello et al., 2005; Leier et al., 2012; Poschet et al., 2007; and Vaandrager et al., 1997.

claims.claim: Previous studies of mouse derived intestinal organoids showed that agonists of PKG are effective in enhancing CFTR-mediated organoid swelling, in the absence of agonists of the canonical regulation of CFTR, such as PKA.
claims.source: Previous studies of mouse derived intestinal organoids showed that agonists of PKG are effective in enhancing CFTR-mediated organoid swelling, in the absence of agonists of the canonical regulation of CFTR, such as PKA (Pattison et al., 2016; Picciotto et al., 1992; Seidler et al., 1997; Vaandrager et al., 1997).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Pattison et al., 2016; Picciotto et al., 1992; Seidler et al., 1997; and Vaandrager et al., 1997.

claims.claim: PKG-mediated phosphorylation exerts a 'priming' effect on the canonical PKA-mediated activation of CFTR.
claims.source: Our studies confirm the functional significance of this regulatory pathway in murine colon, and further, our findings suggest that PKG-mediated phosphorylation exerts a 'priming' effect on the canonical PKA-mediated activation of CFTR.
claims.evidence: Inferred from experiments showing that NO/cGMP enhances PKA-mediated CFTR activation.

claims.claim: There are five sites at which CFTR can be phosphorylated by PKG.
claims.source: There are five sites at which CFTR can be phosphorylated by PKG (NetPhosK v3, consensus strength >0.5).
claims.evidence: Predicted by NetPhosK v3 bioinformatics tool.

claims.claim: Two PKG phosphorylation sites are localized in the regulatory 'R' domain of CFTR, at position 788 and 795, which overlap with the consensus site for PKA phosphorylation.
claims.source: Two are localized in the regulatory 'R' domain, at position 788 and 795, which overlap with the consensus site for PKA phosphorylation (Pasyk et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Pasyk et al., 2015 and bioinformatics prediction.

claims.claim: The strength of the consensus sites for PKG at position 788 is predicted to exceed that of PKA, and may be preferentially phosphorylated by PKG.
claims.source: Interestingly, the strength of the consensus sites for PKG at position 788 is predicted to exceed that of PKA, and may be preferentially phosphorylated by PKG.
claims.evidence: Predicted by bioinformatics analysis of phosphorylation consensus sites.

claims.claim: cGMP partially rescued the defects in cAMP-induced channel activation and organoid swelling in colonic tissue lacking SLC6A14.
claims.source: Both of our assays of regulated F508del-CFTR channel function in colonic tissue lacking SLC6A14 showed that cGMP partially rescued the defects in cAMP-induced channel activation and organoid swelling.

results.result: SLC6A14 is predominantly expressed in the mouse colon, localizes to the apical membrane, and constitutes a major apical arginine uptake pathway. Knockout of Slc6a14 results in ~75% reduction in apical arginine transport and lower steady-state arginine levels in colonic epithelium.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C5 provide converging evidence from qRT-PCR (C1), confocal microscopy (C2), ex vivo transport assays (C3), and mass spectrometry (C5) that collectively demonstrate SLC6A14's role as a major apical arginine transporter in the colon. The data are internally consistent and use appropriate methodologies.

results.result: Loss of Slc6a14 impairs arginine uptake and cAMP-mediated fluid secretion in wild-type mice but does not affect serum amino acid levels, suggesting a dominant role in CFTR regulation rather than nutrient uptake.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C54, and C55 demonstrate that despite reduced colonic arginine uptake, serum amino acid levels remain unchanged, supporting the inference that SLC6A14's primary role in the colon is regulatory rather than nutritional. The logic is sound given that amino acid absorption occurs primarily in the small intestine.

results.result: Disruption of Slc6a14 in CF mice (F508del/F508del) exacerbates post-weaning weight loss and BMI reduction, with temporary growth defects recovering by day 56 but associated with increased mortality during the post-weaning period.
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C11 are supported by longitudinal weight measurements and survival analysis (Figure 2). The data show statistically significant differences in weight, BMI, and survival between double mutant and F508del mice. The temporary nature of the weight defect is clearly documented.

results.result: Loss of Slc6a14 worsens CF-related intestinal phenotypes, including smooth muscle thickening in the distal ileum and colon, and defective secretory capacity.
results.evaluation: Claims C12 and C52 are supported by histological analysis (Figure 3) showing increased smooth muscle area in double mutant mice compared to F508del mice. Statistical significance is demonstrated with appropriate controls.

results.result: Disruption of Slc6a14 further impairs cAMP-induced CFTR-mediated fluid secretion in CF mice, as measured by in vivo closed loop assays and organoid swelling assays, independent of changes in Cftr mRNA expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C13-C17 are supported by multiple complementary assays (in vivo closed loop and organoid swelling) showing consistent worsening of fluid secretion defects in double mutant mice. The exclusion of transcriptional effects (C16) strengthens the conclusion that the effect is post-transcriptional.

results.result: Acute apical arginine addition enhances residual F508del-CFTR channel function in split-open organoids at both 27°C and 37°C in an SLC6A14-dependent manner, with double mutant organoids showing lower baseline cAMP-stimulated CFTR function.
results.evaluation: Claims C18-C23 are supported by ACC assay data at both temperatures (Figure 5). The SLC6A14-dependence is demonstrated by loss of arginine enhancement in double mutant organoids. The use of split-open organoids provides appropriate apical access for testing the hypothesis.

results.result: SLC6A14 overexpression does not affect F508del-CFTR protein processing, cell surface stability, or direct protein-protein interaction, suggesting an indirect mechanism of action.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C27 are supported by western blot, cycloheximide chase, and co-immunoprecipitation experiments (Figure 5 supplements 3-4). The negative results are important for ruling out direct trafficking or stability effects and support a signaling-based mechanism.

results.result: SLC6A14-mediated arginine uptake drives nitric oxide synthesis via iNOS, and this NO production is required for arginine-dependent enhancement of F508del-CFTR function. Slc6a14 knockout mice show reduced constitutive NO levels and abolished arginine-stimulated NO production.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C35 provide a mechanistic link between SLC6A14 and CFTR function through NO signaling. The evidence includes iNOS expression (C28), NO donor effects (C29-C30), iNOS inhibitor studies (C31-C32), and direct NO measurements (C33-C34). The DAF-FM assay is appropriate for NO detection.

results.result: Overexpression of SLC6A14 increases constitutive NO levels and enhances arginine-stimulated NO production in colonic organoids.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C37 provide gain-of-function evidence complementing the loss-of-function studies. The data from lentiviral transduction experiments (Figure 6g-i) show increased NO levels with SLC6A14 overexpression, supporting the causal relationship.

results.result: In Caco-2 cells, PKA-mediated activation of wild-type CFTR is enhanced by NO donors (GSNO, SNP) and cGMP through PKG-dependent signaling, as demonstrated by abolition of the effect with PKG inhibitors.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C40 are supported by pharmacological studies in Caco-2 cells (Figure 7b-d) using NO donors and PKG inhibitors. The use of multiple inhibitors (Rp-8-pCPT-cGMPS and KT5823) addresses specificity concerns. The data establish the NO-cGMP-PKG pathway in human colonic cells.

results.result: In Caco-2 cells overexpressing SLC6A14, arginine-mediated enhancement of CFTR function is blocked by PKG inhibitors and iNOS inhibitor, demonstrating that SLC6A14-mediated arginine transport enhances CFTR function via the NO signaling pathway.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C43 integrate the SLC6A14-arginine-NO-PKG pathway in a human cell model. The data (Figure 7e-f) show that arginine enhancement requires SLC6A14 expression and is sensitive to both iNOS and PKG inhibition, providing strong mechanistic evidence.

results.result: Membrane-permeable cGMP (8Br-cGMP) partially rescues F508del-CFTR channel function and organoid swelling in double mutant mice at both 27°C and 37°C, restoring approximately 50% of F508del-CFTR function at physiological temperature.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C47 demonstrate that bypassing the arginine-NO step with exogenous cGMP can partially rescue the defect in double mutant mice. The data from ACC assay (Figure 8a-b) and organoid swelling (Figure 8c-d) at physiological temperature provide strong support for the proposed signaling pathway.

results.result: SLC6A14 is a major arginine transporter on the apical surface of colonic epithelium in F508del mice, and its arginine transport function ameliorates the basic defect in fluid secretion in CF.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C49 represent the main conclusions of the study, synthesizing findings from multiple experiments. The evidence from transport assays, functional studies, and rescue experiments collectively support these conclusions.

results.result: SLC6A14 has been identified as a genetic modifier of multiple CF disease outcomes (meconium ileus, lung disease, Pseudomonas infection), and its pleiotropic effects support the hypothesis that it modifies the basic defect in anion conduction across multiple organs.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C51 are supported by citations to multiple GWAS studies. The inference that pleiotropic effects suggest modification of the basic defect is logical, though the current study only directly tests intestinal phenotypes.

results.result: Disruption of Slc6a14 in wild-type mice does not cause profound changes in colonic morphology, function, or survival, but does impair arginine uptake and cAMP-mediated fluid secretion, suggesting a regulatory role rather than a nutritional role.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C55 are supported by data from wild-type Slc6a14 knockout mice showing functional defects without gross morphological changes. The inference about regulatory vs. nutritional roles is reasonable given the anatomical distribution of amino acid absorption.

results.result: The F508del mutation in mouse CFTR has less severe consequences on protein folding and trafficking than in human CFTR, resulting in residual epithelial expression and function in mice.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C57 are supported by multiple citations to prior literature. This is established knowledge in the CF field and provides important context for interpreting the mouse model results.

results.result: The modulation of F508del-CFTR by SLC6A14 depends on arginine-mediated NO production and PKG activation, with PKG-mediated phosphorylation exerting a 'priming' effect on PKA-mediated CFTR activation. This pathway has been well-studied in CF models.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C63 synthesize the mechanistic findings with prior literature. The 'priming' model is supported by the experimental data showing that NO/cGMP enhances PKA-mediated activation. The citations provide appropriate context.

results.result: Bioinformatic analysis predicts five PKG phosphorylation sites on CFTR, with two in the regulatory R domain (positions 788 and 795) overlapping with PKA sites, and the PKG consensus at position 788 predicted to be stronger than the PKA consensus.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C66 are based on bioinformatic predictions using NetPhosK v3. While the predictions are reasonable, they are not experimentally validated in this study. The functional significance of these predicted sites remains to be tested. This represents a hypothesis rather than a demonstrated result.

results.result: cGMP partially but incompletely rescues F508del-CFTR function defects in double mutant colonic tissue, suggesting additional unidentified signaling pathways may be involved in SLC6A14-mediated CFTR modulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C68 accurately describe the incomplete rescue by cGMP (Figure 8). The observation that rescue is partial (approximately 50%) is clearly documented and appropriately interpreted as suggesting additional mechanisms may exist.

results.result: The incomplete rescue by cGMP could be explained by other unidentified signaling pathways or by secondary chronic consequences in double mutant mice that impact F508del-CFTR.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C70 are speculative explanations for the incomplete rescue. While these are reasonable hypotheses, they are not tested in the current study. The authors appropriately present these as possibilities requiring future investigation.

results.result: CF patients have decreased exhaled NO related to decreased iNOS activity, increased arginase activity, and decreased arginine bioavailability, though the mechanism underlying decreased arginine bioavailability is unknown.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C74 are supported by citations to prior clinical studies. This provides important context for the current findings, though the mechanism remains unknown as stated.

results.result: The authors propose that decreased arginine bioavailability in CF worsens F508del-CFTR channel function, and that increased SLC6A14 expression would offset this deficit by enhancing NO and cGMP-mediated priming of F508del-CFTR.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C77 are speculative proposals based on the experimental findings. While the logic is sound given the demonstrated mechanism, these predictions have not been tested in CF patients or with interventions to increase SLC6A14 expression. This represents a hypothesis for future testing.

results.result: Bacterial products enhance SLC6A14 expression in CF airway epithelium, and given the high bacterial load in the colon, SLC6A14 expression is expected to be upregulated and positioned to modify mutant CFTR function.
results.evaluation: Claim C78 is supported by citation to prior work in airway epithelium. However, claims C79-C80 extrapolate this to the colon without direct experimental evidence. While the inference is reasonable, it remains speculative without direct measurement of SLC6A14 expression in CF patient colon tissue.

results.result: The extent of SLC6A14 modulation in CF patients will depend on residual F508del-CFTR expression or surface abundance after corrector therapy, and upregulation of SLC6A14 expression may ameliorate CF disease phenotype, though the dependence on GWAS-identified SNP genotypes remains to be determined.
results.evaluation: Claims C58, C71, and C81 are predictions and future directions based on the current findings. While these are logical extensions of the work, they have not been tested experimentally. These represent hypotheses requiring clinical validation.

results.result: Background information on CF disease, CFTR function, disease variability, genetic modifiers, mouse models, and SLC6A14 as a transporter provides context for the study.
results.evaluation: Claims C7 and C82-C104 provide background information supported by appropriate citations to established literature. These claims establish the scientific context and rationale for the study.
